title: Road safety: conflicts, time to collision and rare events
summary: Crashes are rare, so safety studies use near misses. Physics gives surrogate measures such as time to collision; machine learning detects conflicts in video at scale; together they estimate risk before crashes happen.
outcomes: compute time to collision and the deceleration needed to avoid a crash
explain why conflicts are used as surrogates for crashes
describe how computer vision extracts conflicts from video
outline how rare-event (extreme value) models link conflicts to crash risk
narration_en: Road safety has a data problem. Crashes are thankfully rare, so waiting for enough of them to judge a new junction design takes years, and every data point is a tragedy. The alternative is to study near misses, also called traffic conflicts. Physics defines them precisely. Time to collision is the gap between two vehicles divided by their closing speed: how many seconds until impact if nobody changes course. A minimum time to collision below about one and a half seconds is a serious conflict. The deceleration rate to avoid a crash, called DRAC, measures how hard someone must brake. Machine learning makes this practical at scale: object detectors and trackers turn hours of traffic video into vehicle trajectories, and the physics measures are computed automatically. Conflicts happen far more often than crashes, and in our simulation the site with shorter gaps has both more conflicts and more crashes. Extreme value theory then links the frequency of severe conflicts to the probability of crashes. In this module you will change gap, speed, reaction and braking and watch time to collision drop.
narration_ar: تعاني السلامة المرورية من مشكلة في البيانات. فالحوادث، لحسن الحظ، نادرة، لذا فإن انتظار عدد كافٍ منها للحكم على تصميم تقاطع جديد يستغرق سنوات، وكل نقطة بيانات مأساة. والبديل هو دراسة الحوادث الوشيكة، وتسمى أيضاً التعارضات المرورية. والفيزياء تعرّفها بدقة. فالزمن حتى الاصطدام هو المسافة بين مركبتين مقسومة على سرعة اقترابهما: كم ثانية تبقى حتى الاصطدام إذا لم يغيّر أحد مساره. والزمن الأدنى حتى الاصطدام الذي يقل عن ثانية ونصف تقريباً يُعد تعارضاً خطيراً. ومعدل التباطؤ اللازم لتجنب الاصطدام يقيس مدى شدة الكبح المطلوبة. ويجعل تعلم الآلة هذا ممكناً على نطاق واسع: فكواشف الأجسام وأدوات التتبع تحوّل ساعات من فيديو المرور إلى مسارات مركبات، وتُحسب المقاييس الفيزيائية تلقائياً. والتعارضات تحدث أكثر بكثير من الحوادث، وفي محاكاتنا يكون للموقع ذي المسافات الأقصر تعارضات أكثر وحوادث أكثر معاً. ثم تربط نظرية القيم المتطرفة تكرار التعارضات الشديدة باحتمال وقوع الحوادث. ستغيّر في هذه الوحدة المسافة والسرعة وزمن الاستجابة والكبح وتشاهد الزمن حتى الاصطدام ينخفض.

diagram.title: From video to risk
diagram.caption: Vision extracts trajectories, physics measures conflicts, statistics links conflicts to crash risk.

nodes.label: Video and sensors
nodes.detail: Hours of footage from junctions and roads; drones give a top-down view.

nodes.label: Computer vision
nodes.detail: Object detectors (e.g. YOLO) and trackers turn pixels into vehicle and pedestrian trajectories.

nodes.label: Surrogate measures
nodes.detail: TTC = gap/closing speed; post-encroachment time (PET) at crossings; DRAC = closing speed²/(2 gap).

nodes.label: Conflicts
nodes.detail: Events below a threshold. Far more frequent than crashes, so observable in days.

nodes.label: Rare-event model
nodes.detail: Fit the tail of the conflict-severity distribution to estimate crash probability (e.g. Songchitruksa and Tarko 2006).

nodes.label: Safety decisions
nodes.detail: Compare designs or interventions before crashes accumulate.

tour.text: Cameras record traffic; computer vision extracts trajectories.
Physics turns trajectories into surrogate safety measures.
Events below a threshold are counted as conflicts.
Rare-event statistics link conflicts to crash risk.

sections.heading: Time to collision and DRAC
sections.html: For a follower closing on a leader: TTC = gap / (vfollower − vleader) while closing. DRAC = (closing speed)² / (2 × gap), the constant deceleration needed to avoid impact. In the explorer, a 40 m gap closing at 8 m/s with a 1.5 s reaction and 4 m/s² braking reaches a minimum TTC of 3.5 s (safe); with a 20 m gap the minimum TTC is 0.29 s and DRAC is 4 m/s² (serious conflict).

sections.heading: Why conflicts
sections.html: The safety pyramid (Hydén 1987): many undisturbed passages, fewer slight conflicts, fewer serious conflicts, very few crashes. In the lab's simulation of 6,000 encounters, conflicts with TTC below 3 s are 10 to 55 times more frequent than crashes, and the site with shorter gaps has more of both (TTC < 3 s: 7% → 19%; crashes: 0.13% → 1.9%). Conflicts give statistical power in days instead of years.

sections.heading: Machine learning at scale
sections.html: Deep-learning detectors and multi-object trackers extract trajectories from video; physics computes TTC and PET on every interaction; anomaly detection flags unusual manoeuvres. Errors in tracking propagate into the measures, so trajectory smoothing and validation against manual annotation are essential. Physics-informed trajectory reconstruction (vehicles cannot teleport or accelerate at 3 g) removes tracking artefacts.

sections.heading: From conflicts to crash risk
sections.html: Extreme value theory models the tail of conflict severity (for example, the distribution of negative TTC or of required deceleration beyond a threshold) and extrapolates to the point where a crash occurs. It requires careful threshold choice and validation against crash records; simple tails can be badly wrong. Bayesian hierarchical versions pool across sites (Zheng, Sayed and colleagues). This is an active research area.

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html: Keep the gap at 40 m and raise the reaction time from 1.5 to 3 s. When does the outcome change from safe to conflict to crash?

callouts.title: Research angle
callouts.html: Open question: which surrogate measure (TTC, PET, DRAC or learned risk scores) best predicts crashes for vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists?

code.title: Conflicts and crashes at two sites
code.explain: 6,000 simulated encounters per site with random gaps, speeds, reaction times and braking.
code.expected:
site A (longer gaps) : TTC < 3 s  7.32%, TTC < 1.5 s  0.52%, crashes 0.133%, conflicts (TTC < 3 s) per crash  54.9
site B (shorter gaps): TTC < 3 s 19.03%, TTC < 1.5 s  5.48%, crashes 1.850%, conflicts (TTC < 3 s) per crash  10.3

takeaways: Crashes are rare, so safety studies use conflicts measured by physics.
TTC = gap/closing speed; DRAC = closing speed²/(2 gap).
Computer vision extracts trajectories at scale; physics-informed smoothing removes artefacts.
Extreme value models link conflict severity to crash risk but need careful validation.

quiz.q: A minimum TTC below about 1.5 s usually indicates…
Why use conflicts instead of crashes?
options: Conflicts are far more frequent, giving data quickly
Conflicts are easier to define legally

quiz.q: What does extreme value theory model?
options: The tail of conflict severity, to extrapolate to crashes

glossary.def: An event in which road users would collide unless one changes course or speed.
Time until impact if current speeds and paths continue.
Time between one road user leaving a conflict point and another arriving.
Deceleration rate needed to avoid a crash.
Statistics of rare, extreme events, used to link conflicts to crashes.
